accroche: In Lower Bavaria, where Protestants make up less than 1% of the population, their suicide rate climbs to 528% of that of Catholics
contenu_vulgarise:
A man takes his own life. Nothing seems more intimate, more foreign to any collective cause: a despair, a personal history, sometimes a note left on a table. Yet it is on suicide that Émile Durkheim chooses, in 1897, to stake the existence of sociology as an autonomous science.

## The Mechanism

Durkheim compiles suicide statistics from several European countries and cross-references them with the religious confession of the populations. The result is sharply disproportionate: in regions of Bavaria with a very large Catholic majority, where Protestants sometimes make up fewer than one inhabitant in a hundred, he finds as many as 300, 423, even 528 Protestant suicides for every 100 Catholic suicides. From one year to the next, for a given group, this rate barely varies, whereas individual motives have nothing in common from one case to another.

Durkheim rules out explaining this by a Protestant character trait: he attributes it to the degree of integration that each confession imposes on its followers. Protestantism leaves each person to interpret Scripture alone; Catholicism frames a tightly knit community, ritual after ritual. The less an individual is integrated into a group that exceeds and constrains him, the more exposed he is to suicide, a result he also finds among single people compared with married people, or in times of economic crisis compared with stable periods.

This is where the central concept of *Les Règles de la méthode sociologique* (*The Rules of Sociological Method*), published two years earlier, lodges: the social fact. A way of acting, thinking, or feeling that is external to individual consciences and imposes itself on them with a force of constraint: law, language, money, but just as much a suicide rate. A social fact is never explained by the psychology of this or that individual; it is explained by another social fact.

## What It Shifts

The argument is cunning, and that is precisely why Durkheim chooses it: if even the act that seems most radically personal obeys statistical regularities independent of individual wills, then no human phenomenon escapes a properly social explanation. Suicide becomes the test of strength that establishes sociology as a discipline in its own right, with its own causes and methods, neither a mere application of psychology nor a by-product of biology or geography.

The reasoning nevertheless leaves open a question that Durkheim never claimed to settle: why does this particular individual take his own life, in a population subject to the same integration deficit as the majority who do not succumb? The regularity of the collective rate never explains the singular act; it accounts for only one thing: why, from one year to the next, this rate does not move.

repere.texte: In Lower Bavaria, where Protestants did not make up one inhabitant in a hundred, their suicide rate reached 528% of that of Catholics.
repere.source: Durkheim, Le Suicide (Suicide), 1897, Book II, Chapter II

carte.punch: Lower Bavaria: less than 1% Protestants, but 528% of the suicides compared with Catholics.
carte.idee: Durkheim cross-references suicide statistics from several countries with religious confession: Protestants take their own lives far more than Catholics, which he attributes to weaker integration into the community. For him, even the most intimate act obeys statistical regularities.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The complete work, digitized and free of copyright.

quiz.question: Why does Durkheim explain the higher suicide rate among Protestants than among Catholics?
choix: Because the statistics of the time undercounted Catholic suicides
Because the Protestant religion explicitly encourages individual despair
Because Protestantism integrates its followers less strongly into a community that frames their existence
Because Protestants lived in poorer regions in the 19th century
quiz.explication: The rate is due neither to a counting bias, nor to poverty, nor to a religious encouragement of despair: Durkheim attributes it to the weaker collective framing that Protestantism imposes, which leaves each person more alone in the face of life's trials.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In which other cases does Durkheim find the same result, weaker integration and more frequent suicide?
choix: Among single people compared with married people, and in times of economic crisis compared with stable periods
Among city dwellers compared with country dwellers
Among men compared with women, at every age
Among practicing Catholics compared with nonpracticing Catholics
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Durkheim finds the same pattern among single people compared with married people, and in periods of economic crisis compared with stable periods: two situations in which the bond to a group that both constrains and supports loosens.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is a social fact, as defined in The Rules of Sociological Method?
choix: A rare event that upsets the organization of a society
A religious belief shared by the majority of a population
A way of acting or feeling that is external to consciences and imposes itself on them
A decision made collectively by a small group of individuals
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Durkheim defines the social fact as a way of acting, thinking, or feeling that is external to individual consciences and imposes itself on them with a force of constraint: law, language, money, or a suicide rate.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Durkheim choose suicide in particular to establish sociology as an autonomous science?
choix: Because it is the most frequent social phenomenon of his time
Because even the act that seems most personal obeys collective regularities independent of wills
Because suicide statistics were the only ones available at the time
Because suicide was then an offense, which made it easier to collect judicial data
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The argument is cunning, and that is why Durkheim chooses it: if even suicide obeys statistical regularities independent of individual wills, then no human phenomenon escapes a social explanation.
